1.definition: The Zafarnama ("Book of Victory"), the official Timurid history of Timur's campaigns, compiled in 1424 by the court historian Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi. It is the primary Persian-language source for Timur's career, written under Timurid patronage and deliberately propagandistic in framing.

Sultan Mahmud (ruled nominally 1388–1402), the second of Timur's Chagatai puppet khans. He held no real power — Timur governed as his chief military officer — but his name appeared on coins and in official decrees to provide the Genghisid legitimacy Timur lacked.

Timur's mother, a noblewoman of the Barlas clan of Transoxiana. Little is recorded about her beyond her name and lineage; like most women of the fourteenth-century steppe aristocracy she appears only at the edges of the chronicle record.

One of the Turco-Mongol tribal clans of the Chagatai confederation in Transoxiana, alongside the Barlas, Jalayir, and Suldus. The Arlat held grazing land and tribal followers and competed with rival emirs for control of the rich farmland around Samarkand.

"Great commander" — an Arabic-derived military title (literally amir, "commander," plus kabir, "great"). Timur adopted it precisely because, unlike Khan, it carried no requirement of Genghisid descent, so he could use it legitimately while never claiming the royal title itself.

"Lord of the Auspicious Conjunction" — an honorific Timur's court historians applied to him, referring to a favorable astrological alignment of planets said to have occurred at his birth and read as a sign that he was destined to be a world-conqueror.

The "Memoirs of Timur," a first-person autobiography purporting to be dictated by Timur himself. Modern scholars regard it as a sixteenth-century forgery rather than a genuine source, though it shaped the later legend of the conqueror.

"Royal son-in-law" — a Mongol honorific for a man who married a princess of the Genghisid line. It was the closest a non-Genghisid like Timur could come to royal legitimacy, and he used it on his coins and documents. The later Mughals turned it into their dynastic name, Gurkani.

5.definition: A Persian wife of Khalil Sultan (Timur's grandson), on whom he lavished the imperial treasury after seizing Samarkand in 1405. The chroniclers blame her and her relatives for the extravagance that alienated the senior Timurid emirs and helped wreck Khalil Sultan's rule.

7.definition: Vasily Vyatkin was a Russian archaeologist who in 1908 rediscovered and began excavating the lost site of Ulugh Beg's great astronomical observatory near Samarkand, whose location had been forgotten for centuries.

7.matchText: calculated pi to sixteen decimal places

7.definition: The Miftah al-Hisab ("Key of Arithmetic"), an influential mathematical textbook by Jamshid al-Kashi (c. 1380–1429), Ulugh Beg's senior mathematical advisor at the Samarkand observatory. It covered decimal fractions, trigonometry, and root extraction, and was one of the most widely used Islamic mathematical texts.

8.definition: A son of Sultan Abu Sa'id Mirza who ruled Samarkand and Transoxiana as one of the rival Timurid principalities after his father's death in 1469. His line held the central Timurid lands until the Uzbek conquest swept them away around 1500.

"Royal son-in-law" — the Mongol honorific Timur earned by marrying a Genghisid princess; the title gave a non-Genghisid the nearest thing to royal legitimacy. The Mughals later turned it into their dynastic name, Gurkani.
